query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high-throughput DSC system integrated with in-situ neutron imaging can reliably determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change during melting for a broad range of single-phase high-entropy alloys with an accuracy of ±5 °C for melting temperature, 5–10% error for enthalpy/entropy, and 2–3% accuracy for volume change measurements.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., fcc, bcc, or hcp structured systems such as AlxCoCrFeNi, Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr) prepared through conventional metallurgical processing methods to ensure compositional homogeneity.
generation.intervention: Perform differential scanning calorimetry under controlled heating/cooling protocols while simultaneously collecting neutron radiographic images at defined temperature intervals.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in inert atmospheres (e.g., Argon) with heating rates of 5–20 °C/min, spanning from room temperature to temperatures safely above the alloy melting point; neutron imaging frames are captured every ~20 °C to monitor structural changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The correlation of DSC heat flow curves with real-time neutron imaging data that reveals melt pool morphology and density changes during the transition serves as the mediator linking calorimetric and structural information.
generation.mechanism: Heat flow detected by DSC is integrated to extract latent heat, from which enthalpy and entropy of fusion are computed. In parallel, neutron imaging quantifies volume changes and melt morphology, allowing calibration of DSC data against geometric changes. This dual measurement minimizes uncertainties inherent in high‐temperature thermal analysis when used alone.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to yield melting temperatures within ±5 °C, latent heat (enthalpy) and fusion entropy values within 5–10% error, and volume change measurements within 2–3% error across various HEA compositions. In cases where overlapping thermal events or rapid phase transformations occur, deviations beyond these error margins would indicate limitations of the method.
generation.baseline: Reference measurements obtained from standardized DSC protocols using well-characterized melting standards (e.g., pure metals and ceramics) and previous neutron imaging studies on known HEA systems.
generation.boundary: The method is most applicable to single-phase, compositionally homogeneous HEAs; complex multiphase systems or alloys with significant segregation may present challenges due to overlapping thermal signals and reduced neutron imaging contrast.
generation.uncertainty: While the integration of DSC and neutron imaging is promising, uncertainties remain in calibrating the system for extremely rapid or non-equilibrium transitions, and in extending the method to alloys with pronounced multiphase behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct experiments on a set of HEA samples with known melting properties using the integrated DSC-neutron imaging system. Compare measured values (melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume change) with those obtained from established bulk methods using standard references.
measurements: DSC heat flow curves over the melting transition
Neutron radiographic images recorded at ~20 °C intervals
Calibrated standard reference data for melting parameters (e.g., pure metal standards)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured melting temperatures deviate by more than ±5 °C or if the derived enthalpy/entropy values and volume change measurements exceed a 10% and 3% error margin, respectively, relative to established benchmarks, then the proposed integrated method would be ruled out as insufficiently accurate.

An entropy-driven solid–solid transformation is similar to melting, thus requires heat from an external source. To test this possibility, the phase transformation in formulation E1 can be co-analysed with differential scanning calorimetry and in situ temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction using identical heating rates. The data for both measurements are shown in Fig. 3. Figure 3a is a map of diffracted intensity versus diffraction angle (abscissa) as a function of temperature. It covers ∼4° of 2θ space centred about the 111 reflection for E1. At a temperature interval between 825 and 875 °C, there is a distinct transition to single-phase rocksalt structure—all diffraction events in that range collapse into an intense <111> rocksalt peak.

Laser-melted beads, 100–140 mg in weight were placed in tungsten crucibles and sealed under Ar atmosphere to avoid the possibility of sample and standards contamination with carbon vapor from vitreous carbon protection tube. Multiple measurements were performed on each sample. Temperatures of phase transformations were determined as average from the onset [] of endothermic peaks on heating. AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. AbstractReal-time neutron imaging was utilized to produce a movie-like series of radiographs for in-situ observation of the remixing of liquid state immiscibility that occurs in equiatomic CoCrCu with the addition of Ni. A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. Neutron imaging was simultaneously carried out to capture 10 radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back down to 1000 °C. This, in turn, produced a movie-like series of radiographs that allow for the observation of the buttons melting, the transition from immiscible to miscible as Ni is alloyed into the CoCrCu system, and solidification. The components present in CoCrCuFeNi have been shown to phase separate when present in ternary or quaternary combinations. For example, the equiatomic ternary CoCrCu has been shown to phase separate in the liquid [,], indicating the existence of a stable miscibility gap. Equiatomic additions of Ni to CoCrCu have been shown to eliminate LPS and lead to typical dendritic solidification in the CoCrCuNi alloy []. In contrast, additions of Fe to CoCrCu have led to stable LPS which is characterized by macroscopic globule-like phase separations present in the microstructure [,]. This would lead one to believe that the Ni addition in the CoCrCuFeNi alloy is what stabilizes the solution into a single-phase liquid as CoCrCu [] and CoCrCuFe [,] exhibit stable LPS. However, LPS has also been observed in induction-melted CoCrCuFexNi when x = 0.5 [] but not when x = 0 (CoCrCuNi, arc-melted) [] or x = 1 (CoCrCuFeNi, arc-melted) []. When Ni is varied, in the case of arc-melted CoCrCuFeNi0.5, stable LPS is also observed []. It is not immediately clear whether the LPS observed in these alloys is a result of processing parameters or from elemental concentration.

The CoCrCuNi alloy has been previously shown to solidify into a uniform dendritic microstructure from arc-melting [], which is indicative that the microstructure evolved from a single-phase liquid as opposed to the large-scale macroscopic-phase separation that has been observed in similar alloys of CoCrCu [] and CoCrCuFe []. However, there are no reported slow cooling solidification studies on the CoCrCuNi alloy. Previous neutron imaging of the CoCrCu by the present authors resulted in neutron radiographs of the CoCrCu displaying the buttons melting and separating based on density []. The stacking of the liquid immiscible phases of CoCr-rich liquid and Cu-rich liquid was characterized by their differences in neutron attenuation. The same experiment was essentially repeated for this work with the equiatomic addition of Ni buttons such that the equiatomic CoCrCu becomes equiatomic CoCrCuNi once melting and dissolution has occurred. This allows for a more equilibrium solidification due to the slow cooling, as well as an opportunity to image the remixing of the immiscible CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquid phases.

The field of high-entropy alloys continues to grow every year, and with this growth comes an enormous amount of never before seen alloy systems with unknown liquid state behavior. As previously shown, neutron imaging can be a very useful technique to elucidate the liquid state behavior of molten alloy systems. With the application of this technique to high-entropy alloys, in-situ imaging of liquid state miscibility has been observed for the first time with the equiatomic additions of Ni to the immiscible CoCrCu system. The current results show the following: Neutron imaging can be utilized to image liquid state behavior in high-entropy alloys. Imaging was carried out on equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with equiatomic additions of Ni such that when melting occurred between the alloying elements, full miscibility was achieved. In-situ neutron imaging was successfully utilized to image in-situ alloying of Ni into an immiscible CoCrCu system. The synthesis of the CoCrCuNi alloy inside the high-temperature furnace was fully imaged via a movie-like sequence of carefully timed radiographs to display the melting/alloying process. AbstractThe third-generation thermodynamic descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were performed to construct the reliable thermodynamic database for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Laves phase. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both solid and liquid phases were established, from which the thermodynamic properties and thermal vacancy can be well described. The thermodynamic descriptions of Ta-Cr and Ta-V over the whole composition and temperature regions were carried out based on the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) approach. Specifically, the thermodynamic parameters of C14 and C15 Laves phases were evaluated by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as the semiempirical relations. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties in Ta-Cr and Ta-V systems according to the present thermodynamic parameters had a nice agreement with the experimental data even down to 0 K, indicating the reliability of the present modeling.Keywords: third-generation thermodynamic description, Ta-Cr system, Ta-V s

To develop an accurate thermodynamic database over the whole temperature region with physical sense, the concept of a third-generation thermodynamic database has been proposed since 1995 []. Under this framework, several research groups [,,,,,] have made efforts to establish new thermodynamic models for pure elements by using the Debye or Einstein models. Recently, a kind of third-generation thermodynamic model [], which enables one to describe the thermodynamic properties of pure elements down to 0 K as well as thermal vacancy concentration near the melting point, has been proposed by combining the Segmented Regression (SR) model [], two-state model [] and thermal vacancy description []. By applying such a model, a third-generation thermodynamic database for MoNbTaW RHEAs was developed []. To further develop the third-generation thermodynamic databases for Laves containing RHEAs, reliable thermodynamic descriptions for Laves phase are essential. Currently, the reports on third-generation thermodynamic descriptions of Laves phase are rather limited in the literature. Jiang et al. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

proposals.material_system: A broad range of single-phase high-entropy alloys (e.g., fcc-, bcc-, and hcp-structured systems such as AlxCoCrFeNi, Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr, etc.)
proposals.intervention: Develop and deploy a high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) system integrated with in-situ neutron imaging
proposals.conditions: Operate over a temperature interval from room temperature to well above the solidus temperatures (e.g., up to 1600 °C) under controlled atmospheres; utilize standardized heating/cooling rates (e.g., 5–20 °C/min) and synchronize DSC data with neutron radiography frames at ~20 °C steps
proposals.structural_mediator: Real-time observation of phase transition events and melt pool morphology changes
proposals.mechanism: DSC quantifies heat flow to determine latent heat (enthalpy of fusion) and, through integration and calibrated baselines, entropy of fusion. The neutron imaging component tracks density and positional changes to resolve volume change during melting. Combining these measurements addresses the detriments of conventional bulk techniques by allowing simultaneous calorimetric and structural data capture.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Accurate estimates of melting temperature (with ±5 °C precision), latent heat (enthalpy) within 5–10% error, entropy of fusion calculated from integrated DSC curves, and volume change measured to within 2–3% accuracy across various HEA compositions. Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties (e.g., heat capacity) would be resolved in real time.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach provides an efficient, parallel methodology to characterise a wide range of HEAs by directly measuring fusion-related thermodynamic properties while simultaneously imaging the melt structure. It leverages well-established DSC techniques (as in PMC7513177) and innovative neutron imaging (PMC8320920) to overcome limitations in tracking rapid phase transitions and immiscibility phenomena.

proposals.material_system: Refractory high-entropy alloys such as TaNbHfZr
proposals.intervention: Implement a hierarchical computational modelling strategy combining CALPHAD assessments with first-principles (DFT) calculations
proposals.conditions: Calibrate thermodynamic models over the complete composition and temperature range from 0 K to melting (up to 2500 K) using existing databases, and refine parameters via iterative comparison with available experimental data
proposals.structural_mediator: Gibbs energy surfaces and phase diagram features that incorporate configurational and vibrational contributions
proposals.mechanism: The approach uses third-generation Gibbs energy descriptions (as demonstrated in the Ta-Cr and Ta-V systems in PMC8950179) and complements them with ab-initio predictions of liquid structure properties. The combination allows for quantitative prediction of melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase Cp by minimizing free energy differences between phases.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Predicted melting temperatures within 2–3% of measured values; similarly, enthalpy and entropy of fusion determined within a small margin of error (<5% deviation). The approach should have broad applicability to HEAs with different lattice structures by adjusting input parameters based on end-member data.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By integrating CALPHAD with first-principles calculations, this method offers both accuracy (through well-established thermodynamic frameworks) and efficiency (computer simulations) to explore large composition spaces in the HEA family. It also provides a consistent thermodynamic picture that can be validated decisively against experimental phase boundaries.

proposals.material_system: Selected equiatomic HEA systems such as CoCrCu-based alloys, transitioning to quaternary combinations like CoCrCuNi
proposals.intervention: Utilize time-resolved synchrotron X-ray diffraction during rapid laser melting experiments
proposals.conditions: Perform rapid laser melting and subsequent controlled cooling (e.g., cooling rates exceeding 10^3 °C/s) in an inert atmosphere while collecting diffraction patterns in intervals of a few milliseconds over a temperature window spanning pre-melting to complete solidification
proposals.structural_mediator: Transient liquid structure and immediate post-melting atomic arrangements extracted from diffraction peak shifts and broadenings
proposals.mechanism: The laser-induced melting mimics high heating rates and produces a well-defined liquid phase that can be probed in situ. The shifts in diffraction peak positions and intensities will yield precise changes in lattice parameters corresponding to volume expansion, while profile analysis coupled with calorimetric correlations (from existing heat flow data) allows determination of the energetic parameters of melting.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Quantitative determination of melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy of fusion with high temporal (millisecond) and spatial resolution; predicted volume change at melting measured to within a 3% error margin; applicable for HEAs sensitive to rapid thermal cycling and non-equilibrium processing.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach bridges the gap between dynamic structural transformations and thermodynamic measurements under rapid heating conditions, supporting measurements of liquid-phase properties that are otherwise obscured by long equilibration times. It exploits the sensitivity of synchrotron diffraction to capture transient phenomena, thus providing decisive validation if the observed diffraction patterns deviate unexpectedly from equilibrium models.

proposals.material_system: Combinatorial thin-film libraries of high-entropy alloys (e.g., varying compositions within the Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni system)
proposals.intervention: Develop a microcalorimetry platform coupled with rapid combinatorial synthesis (e.g., sputtering) to simultaneously measure melting properties across compositional gradients
proposals.conditions: Fabricate thin-film compositional libraries on microfabricated calorimetric sensors, allowing rapid heating (e.g., rates up to 100 °C/s) in controlled atmospheres from room temperature to melting; integrate high-sensitivity thermometry capable of detecting heat flow in the sub-microjoule range
proposals.structural_mediator: Localized thermal signatures correlated with phase transitions and local compositional fluctuations recorded on microdevices
proposals.mechanism: The microcalorimetric sensors detect minute changes in heat flow associated with melting, from which enthalpy and entropy of fusion can be extracted via integration of the sensor signal. The thin-film format enhances the speed of thermal equilibration and reduces thermal lag, allowing measurement of volume change indirectly through calibration against known standards. This method benefits from the increased configurational entropy inherent to HEA thin films that stabilize single-phase structures.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Efficient, parallel determination of melting temperature (accuracy ±5 °C), enthalpy and entropy of fusion within 5–10% error, and inferred volume change trends across hundreds of composition variants. The method is suited for rapid screening and could become a standard tool in HEA research.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By miniaturizing the experimental setup to a combinatorial format, this approach addresses both the efficiency and accuracy challenges across a wide HEA composition space. It offers decisive validation in the form of reproducible melting signatures; any systematic deviation (e.g., inconsistent heat flow or inability to resolve latent heat) would rule out the approach.

decision.rationale: Direction C directly addresses the research question by combining high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry with in-situ neutron imaging. This integrated approach enables simultaneous measurement of thermal signals (for melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy of fusion) and real‐time imaging of the structural evolution (to capture volume change at melting), thereby providing both accuracy and efficiency in exploring a wide composition space of single-phase HEAs. Previous studies using DSC and neutron imaging (as evident in allowed evidence records) support the feasibility and expected quantitative performance of this method. The decisive validation criterion is whether reproducible and calibrated thermal and structural signatures are obtained; systematic deviations would falsify the approach.
